links.note: Recalls the parallelogram area as the product of its two given dimensions - one of the plane-figure area formulas the chapter treats as already known before it starts on new shapes.
Area of a circle is pi r squared: a formula for a figure the chapter explicitly says is already handled, with the 1/2, 2 and 4 variants as traps.
6a squared, because every one of a cube's six faces is the same square. That collapse of the cuboid formula is this concept.
Volume of a cuboid is lbh - the length-times-breadth-times-height count this concept gives, with the two surface-area expressions offered as distractors.
Perimeter of a rectangle is 2(l+w), one of the already-known boundary formulas rather than the definition of perimeter itself.
15 x 10 = 150 sq cm applies the known rectangle area formula to numbers.

Rhombus area from diagonals 10 and 8.2 is 41 sq cm. The half-product-of-diagonals rule comes from splitting the quadrilateral on a diagonal into two triangles and adding them, which is this concept; the set has no rhombus-specific concept.
Area 240 with one diagonal 16 gives the other as 30 - the same split-into-triangles area rule for a quadrilateral, run backwards for a missing diagonal.
One curved surface and two identical circular faces is exactly what a cylinder shows when it is opened out - two circles and a rectangle.
2(lb + bh + hl) with 20, 15 and 10 gives 1300 sq cm. The formula used is the three-pairs-of-identical-faces reduction of the six face areas.
2 pi r (r + h) = 968 with r = 7 gives h = 15. The total surface area formula being inverted is the one the unrolled cylinder - two circles plus a rectangle - produces.
5.1 x 2 x 2 = 20.4 cubic metres: the lbh volume count applied to decimal dimensions. (The options are printed with m^2 units, which is an extraction slip; the value is right.)
Area 70 with one diagonal 14 gives the other as 10 - the half-product-of-diagonals rule that splitting the quadrilateral into triangles produces.
Area 60 with one diagonal 10 gives the other as 12, again inverting the diagonals rule from the triangle split.

Equal heights and volumes 16 pi and 81 pi give radii in the ratio 4:9, because volume is the base area times the height and only the base area differs. (The marked option renders 4:9 as an Excel serial.)
Names the rhombus area as half the product of the diagonals ('once' is an OCR slip for 'area'). That expression is what adding the two triangles from a diagonal split gives.
A 1 cm edge gives a volume of 1 - the cube of the side, which is the cuboid volume with all three dimensions equal. This concept's special case.
Area of a rectangle is ab, a formula the chapter counts as already known, with a+b and a^2+b^2 as traps.
Area of a triangle is half base times altitude - another of the already-handled figures, the distractors varying only the fraction.
Area of a circle is pi r squared - the same already-known circle formula as qid 113748.
Surface area of a cube is 6a squared: six congruent square faces.
25 x 20 = 500 sq cm, the known rectangle area formula on numbers.
1 kilolitre = 1000 dm cubed, which is the litre-to-cubic-measure relation this concept says has to be known, at kilolitre scale.
Asks for the perimeter of a given figure, i.e. the distance right round its boundary, rather than applying any named formula - the figure itself is not in the extracted text.
